tips.title: Always from the normal
tips.body: Every angle in this topic is measured from the **normal**, the dashed line at right angles to the surface, never from the surface itself. If a question gives an angle to the surface, subtract it from 90° before using it. Drawing the normal first makes the mistake almost impossible.

tips.title: Slower bends towards, faster bends away
tips.body: Decide which way the **speed** goes before you draw anything. Into glass or water the light **slows**, so it bends **towards** the normal. Coming back out it **speeds up** and bends **away**. Along the normal it changes speed but does not bend at all.

tips.title: An object cannot reflect what it is not given
tips.body: For any colour question, list what the object reflects and what the light contains, then take the overlap. No overlap means **black**. This handles a red object in green light, a white page in blue light and every filter question in one move.

tips.title: Frequency is the one that stays
tips.body: When light crosses a boundary the **speed** changes and the **wavelength** changes with it, but the **frequency** does not: the source still makes the same number of waves each second. If your answer changed the frequency, it is wrong.

tips.title: Check the trace before measuring
tips.body: Before reaching for the protractor, check the joined-up trace: the reflected ray should make the **same angle** with the normal as the incoming ray, and the ray leaving the block should be **parallel** to the one going in. If either fails, a cross was marked in the wrong place, and no careful measuring will fix it.

why.matters:
You have never seen an object. You see **light that has left it**, and everything about how something looks is a fact about what its surface did to that light.

That is why these three ideas belong in one topic. **Reflection** decides whether you see the thing itself or a picture of something else in it. **Refraction** decides where it appears to be, which is not always where it is. **Absorption** decides its colour, by removing everything the surface does not send back. Mirrors, glasses, a straw that looks broken and green grass are all the same three answers.

examples.title: Why a wet road dazzles you at night
examples.body:
Dry tarmac is rough at the scale light cares about. Each patch faces its own way, so each has its own normal, and the headlight beam comes back **scattered** — which is what lets you see the road ahead.

Rain fills those dips with water and leaves one flat surface with one normal. Now the reflection is **specular**: the light stays together, oncoming headlights arrive in your eyes as glare, and the road itself goes dark because its light has gone somewhere else. Neither surface breaks the law of reflection. Every ray obeys it; the normals differ.

examples.title: The pool is deeper than it looks
examples.body:
Light leaving the water for the air **speeds up**, so it bends **away from the normal**. Your eye does not know that. It traces the ray it receives back in a straight line, and that line meets the bottom higher up than the bottom really is.

Light goes about 1.33 times faster in air, and that is the factor: a pool 2.0 m deep looks about 1.5 m. Half a metre of it is missing. It is the same bend that snaps a straw in a glass and puts a fish somewhere other than where it appears.

visual.alt: A ray diagram of light leaving water for air at thirty degrees to the normal and bending away from it to about forty two degrees, because it travels faster in the air

examples.title: A red coat under an orange street lamp
examples.body:
The deep-orange street lamps still on some roads are low-pressure sodium, and they give out one narrow band of colour and nothing else. An object can only reflect what it is given.

So a red coat, which reflects red and absorbs the rest, is handed no red at all: it looks **black**. Blue jeans go black for the same reason. A white shirt reflects everything it is given, so it turns orange, and a yellow jacket stays bright because the lamp is almost exactly its colour. The cars are all the same colour too.

steps.title: What happens when light meets a boundary
steps.body:
When a wave arrives at the boundary between two materials, three things can happen to it, and usually all three happen at once in different proportions.

- It can be **reflected**, bouncing back into the first material.
- It can be **absorbed**, transferring its energy to the material.
- It can be **transmitted**, carrying on into the second material.

Which of these dominates depends on the material **and** on the wavelength. A glass window transmits visible light but absorbs most ultraviolet, which is why you do not get sunburnt through a closed window.

A material that transmits light is either **transparent**, which you can see a clear image through, or **translucent**, which lets light through but scatters it so the image is blurred. Frosted bathroom glass is translucent. A material that transmits nothing is **opaque**.

This whole topic is **Physics only**, not combined science.

visuals.alt: Four boxes on what happens to light at a boundary: reflected, absorbed, transmitted, and the difference between transparent, translucent and opaque

steps.title: Reflection, and the normal
steps.body:
To describe reflection you need one construction line that is not the light itself: the **normal**. It is the line drawn at **right angles to the surface** at the point where the ray hits.

Every angle in this topic is measured **from the normal**, never from the surface. That single habit is worth several marks a paper.

The law is short:

$$\text{angle of incidence} = \text{angle of reflection}$$

A ray diagram earns its marks for the details: the normal drawn **dashed** and at right angles, the angles marked **between the ray and the normal**, and an **arrow** on each ray showing which way the light travels.

check.solution: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and both are measured **from the normal**. So the answer is 35°. The 55° option is the angle from the **surface**, which is the classic trap.

steps.title: Specular and diffuse reflection
steps.body:
Both kinds of reflection obey the same law. The difference is the **surface**, not the physics.

- **Specular reflection** happens at a **smooth** surface. Parallel rays arrive, and because the surface has the same normal everywhere, they all reflect **in a single direction**. You see a clear image. A mirror or still water does this.
- **Diffuse reflection** happens at a **rough** surface. Each part of the surface faces a slightly different way, so each ray meets a different normal and reflects at a different angle. The light is **scattered**, and you see no image. Paper, a wall or a wooden table does this.

The mark is lost by saying the rough surface *breaks* the law of reflection. It does not. Every single ray still obeys it. What changes is that the normals point in different directions.

steps.title: Refraction, and why it happens
steps.body:
When light crosses into a different material it usually **changes direction**. That is **refraction**, and the reason is a change in **speed**.

Light travels **more slowly** in glass or water than in air. At the boundary:

- Going into a **slower** material, the ray bends **towards** the normal.
- Going into a **faster** material, the ray bends **away** from the normal.
- A ray travelling **along** the normal, at 0° to it, does not bend at all, though it does still change speed.

At Higher tier you must say *why*, and the answer is always the change of speed, not a vague "the glass is denser".

The wave front picture makes it clear. Imagine the wave fronts as a line of people marching in step. When one end of the line reaches the slow ground first, that end takes shorter steps while the other end is still striding, so the whole line **pivots**. That is exactly what a wave front does at a boundary, and why the direction changes.

steps.title: Required practical 9: tracing a ray through a block
steps.body:
Required practical 9 (physics only) is the ray diagram done for real, with a **ray box** and a **rectangular block** of glass or Perspex.

**Method.**

1. On plain paper draw a straight line with a ruler, then use a protractor to draw the **normal** at right angles to it. Label it N.
2. Put the block against the line and **draw round it**.
3. Fit the **slit** to the ray box so it gives one **narrow** ray, and aim it at the point where the normal meets the block, at an angle to the normal.
4. Mark the path of the **incoming** ray and of the two **outgoing** rays with **crosses**: the one **reflected** off the front face, and the one that comes out of the **far** face after passing through.
5. Switch the ray box off, **remove the block**, and join each pair of crosses with a ruler. The ray **inside** the block is the straight line from where it went in to where it came out.
6. Measure the **angle of incidence**, the **angle of reflection** and the **angle of refraction**, each **from the normal**.
7. Repeat with the other block.

**What you find.** The angle of **reflection equals** the angle of incidence, for every surface. The angle of **refraction is smaller** than the angle of incidence, because the light **slows** in the block and bends **towards** the normal, and it is **different for different materials**: AQA's own measurements at 25° were **17° in glass** and **16° in Perspex**. The ray leaves the far face **parallel** to the way it came in, shifted sideways.

**Different surfaces.** A **smooth** surface, the block's face or a mirror, gives one reflected ray you can trace. A **rough** surface such as white card scatters the light in every direction, so there is no single ray to mark: **diffuse** reflection, though each ray still obeys the law.

**Getting the angles right.** Two things lose accuracy: a **wide** ray, cured by the **slit** and by marking the **centre** of the ray; and crosses marked **close together**, cured by marking them **far apart**, so the joined line's direction is exact. Work in a **dark** room so the faint rays can be seen, and measure to the nearest **degree**.

steps.title: Why an object has a colour
steps.body:
Each colour in the visible spectrum has its **own narrow band of wavelength and frequency**. Red is the long-wavelength end, violet the short.

The colour of an **opaque** object is decided by **which wavelengths it reflects most strongly**. Whatever it does not reflect, it **absorbs**.

- Reflect **all** wavelengths equally and the object looks **white**.
- Absorb **all** wavelengths and it looks **black**.
- Reflect only the red band and absorb the rest, and it looks **red**.

The interesting questions change the light. A red book in white light looks red, because white light contains red for it to reflect. Put the same red book under **green** light and it looks **black**: there is no red in the light to reflect, and the green that arrives is absorbed.

An object cannot reflect a colour that is not shining on it. That one sentence answers most colour questions.

steps.title: Your turn: filters
steps.body:
A **colour filter** works by **absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others**. A red filter transmits red and absorbs the rest.

Work through these, giving a reason each time rather than just an answer.

1. White light passes through a red filter. What comes out?
2. That red light then falls on a **white** page. What colour does the page look?
3. The same red light falls on a **blue** page. What colour does that look?
4. White light passes through a red filter and then a **blue** filter. What comes out, and why?

Part 4 is the one worth thinking hardest about.

steps.title: Going deeper: wave fronts, and refraction explained properly
steps.body:
This explanation is **Higher tier**.

A **wave front** is a line joining points of the wave that are all in step, like the crests of a set of waves rolling in. The rays are at **right angles** to the wave fronts.

When a wave front meets a boundary **at an angle**, one end of it crosses first. Once across, that end travels at the **new, slower speed** while the other end is still moving at the old, faster one. The front therefore **pivots** and ends up travelling in a new direction. The rays, still at right angles to it, have changed direction too.

That is the full explanation, and it tells you two useful things.

- If the wave front arrives **parallel** to the boundary, so every part of it crosses at the same moment, there is nothing to pivot about and the wave carries on undeviated. That is the ray along the normal, which changes speed but not direction.
- The **wavelength** changes at the boundary while the **frequency** stays the same. The source is still producing the same number of waves per second, so from $v = f\lambda$, a slower speed with an unchanged frequency means a **shorter wavelength**.

That last point is the one to reach for when a question asks what happens to the wavelength.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- At a boundary a wave can be **reflected**, **absorbed** or **transmitted**, and which dominates depends on the material and the wavelength.
- A material that transmits light is **transparent** (clear image) or **translucent** (scattered, blurred). One that transmits none is **opaque**.
- Every angle is measured from the **normal**, the line at right angles to the surface.
- **Angle of incidence = angle of reflection**.
- **Specular** reflection is from a **smooth** surface, giving rays in a **single direction** and a clear image. **Diffuse** reflection is from a **rough** surface, **scattering** the rays. Both obey the law of reflection.
- **Refraction** is the change of direction caused by a change of **speed**. Into a slower material, the ray bends **towards** the normal; into a faster one, **away**. Along the normal it does not bend at all.
- Each colour has its **own narrow band** of wavelength and frequency.
- An **opaque** object's colour comes from the wavelengths it **reflects most strongly**; the rest are **absorbed**. All reflected is white, all absorbed is black.
- An object cannot reflect a colour that is not in the light, which is why a red object under green light looks **black**.
- **Filters** absorb some wavelengths and **transmit** others.
- **Higher tier**: a wave front **pivots** because one end crosses the boundary first and slows. The **frequency stays the same**, so the wavelength changes with the speed.
- **Required practical 9**: ray box and slit, draw round the block, mark each ray with crosses **far apart**, remove the block and join them, then measure every angle **from the normal**. Reflection equals incidence; refraction is smaller and differs between materials.

questions.prompt: A student says: "A rough surface does not obey the law of reflection, which is why you cannot see your face in a piece of paper." Explain what is right and what is wrong in this statement.
questions.solution: The student is right that you cannot see your face in a piece of paper, and right that the roughness of the surface is the reason, but wrong to say that the law of reflection is broken. Every individual ray that hits the paper still obeys the law of reflection, so for each ray the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. What makes the difference is that a rough surface has bumps facing in many different directions, so the normal at one point is not parallel to the normal at the next. Parallel rays arriving therefore meet normals pointing different ways and leave at different angles, which scatters the light. This is diffuse reflection, and because the rays no longer travel in a single direction no image is formed.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What is right.** No image forms, and the roughness of the surface is indeed the reason.

**What is wrong.** The law of reflection is **not** broken. **Every individual ray** still obeys it: for each one, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

**The real explanation.** A rough surface has bumps facing many different ways, so the **normal** at one point is not parallel to the normal at the next. Parallel rays arriving therefore meet normals pointing in different directions and leave at different angles. The light is **scattered**, which is **diffuse reflection**, and with no single direction of travel no image forms.

questions.prompt: A red tomato is viewed first under white light and then under blue light. Describe and explain what colour it appears in each case, and explain how a blue filter placed in front of a white lamp produces the blue light.
questions.solution: The colour of an opaque object is determined by which wavelengths it reflects most strongly, and the wavelengths it does not reflect are absorbed. A red tomato reflects the red band of wavelengths and absorbs the others. Under white light, which contains all the wavelengths of the visible spectrum, the red is available for the tomato to reflect, so the tomato appears red. Under blue light the situation is different, because there is no red in the light for the tomato to reflect. The blue light that does arrive is absorbed by the tomato, so no light is reflected from it at all and it appears black. The blue light itself is produced because a colour filter works by absorbing certain wavelengths and transmitting others. A blue filter transmits the blue band and absorbs the rest of the white light from the lamp, so only blue light emerges from it.

criteria.text: States that an opaque object's colour is set by the wavelengths it reflects most strongly
States that white light contains all the wavelengths of the visible spectrum
Concludes that the tomato appears red under white light
Explains that blue light contains no red for the tomato to reflect
Concludes that the tomato appears black, since the blue light is absorbed
Explains that a blue filter absorbs other wavelengths and transmits blue

questions.modelAnswer:
**Under white light.** An opaque object's colour comes from the wavelengths it **reflects most strongly**; the rest are **absorbed**. A red tomato reflects the red band. White light contains **all** the wavelengths, so red is there to be reflected, and the tomato appears **red**.

**Under blue light.** There is **no red** in the light for the tomato to reflect, and the blue that arrives is **absorbed**. Nothing is reflected, so the tomato appears **black**.

**The filter.** A colour filter **absorbs certain wavelengths and transmits others**. A blue filter absorbs everything in the lamp's white light except the blue band, which it transmits, so only blue light emerges.

questions.prompt: In required practical 9, a ray hits the face of a glass block at 25° to the normal. What angle of reflection, in degrees, should be measured?
questions.solution: The angle of **reflection equals** the angle of **incidence**, both measured from the normal: **25°**.

questions.prompt: Why is a slit fitted to the ray box in required practical 9?
questions.solution: A **narrow** ray has a clear centre line to mark with crosses. A wide beam has no single path, so the angles measured from it are uncertain.

markScheme.description: To give a narrow ray that can be marked accurately

options: To stop the ray box from getting too hot
To split the white light into its colours
To give a narrow ray that can be marked accurately
To make the ray bright enough to see with the lights on

questions.prompt: AQA's results for required practical 9: at 25° incidence the angle of refraction was 17° in glass and 16° in Perspex. What does this show?
questions.solution: The more the light **slows**, the more it bends **towards** the normal and the **smaller** the angle of refraction. Perspex gave the smaller angle, so it slows the light slightly **more**. The difference is small but real, and it is why the practical uses two materials.

markScheme.description: Light slows down slightly more in Perspex than in glass

options: Light slows down slightly more in Perspex than in glass
Light slows down slightly more in glass than in Perspex
Light speeds up in both, because the angles are smaller
The two blocks were not placed on the same line

questions.prompt: A student shines the ray at a piece of white card instead of the block and cannot find a reflected ray to mark. Why?
questions.solution: White card is **rough**, so its normals point in many directions and the light is reflected in **all** directions: **diffuse** reflection. There is plenty of reflected light, but no single ray to trace.

markScheme.description: The rough surface scatters the light in every direction

options: White card absorbs all of the light that hits it
The card transmits the light instead of reflecting it
The rough surface scatters the light in every direction
The card reflects the ray straight back along its own path

questions.prompt: A student measures the angle of refraction between the refracted ray and the block's surface, and records 73°. The true angle of refraction is 17°. What should they do?
questions.solution: Angles are measured **from the normal**. The surface is at 90° to the normal, so $90 - 73 = 17°$: the reading is not wrong, it is the wrong angle. Every angle in this topic is taken from the normal.

markScheme.description: Measure from the normal instead, which gives 17°

options: Repeat the reading, because 73° is impossible
Subtract 73° from 180° to get the true angle
Move the ray box round until the reading falls to 17°
Measure from the normal instead, which gives 17°

questions.prompt: A ray is traced through a rectangular block 6.0 cm thick. It leaves the far face 1.8 cm further along than it entered, measured parallel to the faces. Calculate the angle of refraction, in degrees, to the nearest degree.
questions.solution: Inside the block the ray runs straight from entry to exit. Across 6.0 cm it shifts 1.8 cm sideways, so $\tan r = \dfrac{1.8}{6.0} = 0.30$ and $r = 17°$ to the nearest degree.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the refraction of light by two different transparent blocks. Include the measurements you would take, how you would keep the comparison fair, and one way to improve the accuracy of the angles.
questions.solution:
Draw a line on plain paper and a **normal** at right angles to it, place the first block against the line and **draw round it**. Use a **ray box** with a **slit** to send one **narrow** ray at the point where the normal meets the block, at an angle to the normal.

Mark the **incoming** ray and the ray **leaving the far face** with **crosses**, well apart. Remove the block and **join** the crosses; the line from the entry point to the exit point is the ray **inside** the block. Measure the **angle of incidence** and the **angle of refraction** with a protractor, each **from the normal**.

To keep the comparison **fair**, use the **same angle of incidence** for both blocks, against the same line and normal, and the same ray box. Repeat with the second block and compare the two angles of refraction: the material that gives the **smaller** angle slows the light more.

For **accuracy**, mark the **centre** of the ray, put the crosses **far apart** so the joined line's direction is exact, work in a **dark** room so the faint ray can be seen, and read the protractor to the **nearest degree**, repeating and averaging.

examTechnique.body:
Draw the **normal** first, dashed and at right angles, before any ray. Every angle is measured from it, and a question that quotes an angle to the **surface** is testing whether you noticed.

For a ray diagram, use a ruler, mark the angles between ray and normal, and put an **arrow** on each ray.

For refraction, decide which way the **speed** changes first, then the bending follows: slower bends towards the normal, faster bends away. At Higher tier say that the change of direction is **caused by** the change of speed, and remember the frequency does not change.

For colour, write down what the object reflects and what the light contains, then take the overlap. No overlap means black. A filter absorbs some wavelengths and transmits the rest; two different filters in series usually leave nothing.

When an answer involves a rough surface, never say the law of reflection is broken. Say the normals point in different directions.

For required practical 9, describe the crosses **far apart**, the block **removed** before joining them, and every angle measured **from the normal**. Say that the reflected angle **equals** the incident angle and the refracted angle is **smaller**, and that the two blocks give **different** refracted angles for the same incidence.
examinerErrors: Measuring angles from the surface rather than from the normal, so every angle is 90 minus the right one.
Saying a rough surface does not obey the law of reflection. Every ray still obeys it.
Explaining refraction by saying the glass is denser, without mentioning the change of speed.
Bending the ray the wrong way: into a slower material it bends towards the normal.
Saying a red object under green light looks dark red. It looks black, because nothing is reflected.
Claiming a filter turns one colour into another. It absorbs some wavelengths and transmits others.
Saying the frequency changes at a boundary. The speed and wavelength change; the frequency does not.
Drawing rays freehand and without arrows, which loses the accuracy and direction marks.
Marking the crosses close to the block, so the joined line's direction is uncertain.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer draws the normal before anything else and measures every angle from it, so a question quoting an angle to the surface is converted rather than used. For refraction it names the change of speed as the cause, not merely something that also happens, and at Higher tier explains the pivot of the wave front as one end crosses the boundary first. It knows the frequency is fixed by the source and so deduces the wavelength change from the wave equation rather than asserting it. For colour it reasons from what the object reflects and what the light actually contains, and says black without hedging when there is no overlap. And it never accuses a rough surface of breaking the law of reflection.
